A 3-day-old boy is evaluated in the hospital nursery for the delayed passage of meconium. The patient
is breastfed, has been feeding well every 2 hours, and is urinating over 8 times per day. He was born at

35 weeks gestation to a 27-year-old G4P4 mother. The patient is of Ashkenazi Jewish descent and the
patient’s parents refused all prenatal genetic testing. The pregnancy was uncomplicated until the
patient’s mother had a spontaneous rupture of membranes at 35 weeks of gestation. The patient’s 3
older siblings are all healthy. The patient’s temperature is 98.2°F (36.8°C), blood pressure is 89/57
mmHg, pulse is 150/min, and respirations are 44/min. On physical exam, he appears to be in moderate
distress. He has no dysmorphic features, and his abdomen is distended and non-tender. Bowel sounds
are absent. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management? Answer Choices:
(A) Exploratory laparotomy (B) Rectal biopsy (C) Abdominal ultrasound (D) Barium swallow (E)
Abdominal radiograph (F) Measurement of stool elastase (G) Contrast enema (H) Upper
gastrointestinal series (I) Serum lactate levels (J) Genetic testing for CFTR mutations
 A. Barium swallow
B. Abdominal ultrasound
C. Measurement of stool elastase
D. Upper gastrointestinal series
E. Serum lactate levels
F. Exploratory laparotomy
G. Genetic testing for CFTR mutations
H. Contrast enema
I. Abdominal radiograph
J. Rectal biopsy
